summary: Proposes a simple method for workstations to dynamically fetch mail from a mailbox server, which became known as POP3 (Post Office Protocol version 3). It was published as a proposal asking for discussion and improvements. It was replaced by RFC 1225.

eli5.summary: Your mail waits in a big mailbox at a post office. This lets your own computer walk up, ask for your letters, and bring them home.

subtitle: A protocol for workstations to retrieve mail from a server.

tldr.problem: Workstations and personal computers often lack the resources to run a full mail server, but users want to access mail stored on a central server.
tldr.mechanism: POP3 (Post Office Protocol version 3) lets a client connect to a server, authenticate with a username and password, list and retrieve messages, and mark messages for deletion before disconnecting.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1081 was replaced by RFC 1225, which improved the protocol. POP3 remains widely used for mail retrieval.

today: RFC 1081 was replaced by RFC 1225, which made improvements to the protocol. POP3 remains a standard email retrieval protocol used by millions of mail clients and servers decades after this RFC.

sections.title: The Need for Remote Mail Access
sections.content:
Not all computers on the Internet can afford to run a full mail transport system. Workstations may lack sufficient disk space or processing power to run an SMTP server and local mail delivery system continuously. Personal computers may only be connected to the network intermittently and cannot maintain a constantly running mail service. Yet users of these systems want to manage their mail.

The solution is the split-UA model: a central server holds everyone's mail, and lightweight clients connect to retrieve it as needed. POP3 provides the protocol for this mail retrieval. Clients send mail via SMTP to a relay host (which may or may not be the POP3 server), and they fetch mail via POP3 from the server. This divides the user agent functions between two systems, each optimized for its role.
sections.eli5: Some computers do not have room for a post office. Instead, mail waits at a shared post office and your computer asks for it when you want it.

sections.title: Connection States
sections.content:
A POP3 session progresses through three states. The AUTHORIZATION state begins when the TCP connection opens (port 110). The server sends a greeting, and the client must authenticate using the USER command (to provide the username) and PASS command (to provide the password). If authentication succeeds, the server acquires an exclusive lock on the mailbox and the session moves to the TRANSACTION state.

In the TRANSACTION state, the client can issue commands like STAT (to get mailbox statistics), LIST (to list messages), RETR (to retrieve a message), DELE (to mark a message for deletion), and others. When the client issues QUIT, the session enters the UPDATE state. In UPDATE, the server removes all messages marked for deletion, releases the mailbox lock, and closes the connection.
sections.eli5: When you call the post office, you first prove who you are. Then you can ask for mail. When you are done, they throw away any letters you said to throw away.

sections.title: Messages and Commands
sections.content:
After successful authentication, the server parses the mailbox into individual messages and assigns each a message ID starting from 1. The server also tracks the highest message ID accessed by previous sessions using the LAST command. During the TRANSACTION state, the client can retrieve individual messages with RETR, get a list of all messages with LIST, or retrieve just the headers and first few lines of the body with the optional TOP command.

The protocol uses a simple response scheme: all server responses are either +OK (positive) or -ERR (negative) followed by a description. Multi-line responses (such as the full text of a message) are terminated with a line containing only a period. Any line in the message that starts with a period is preceded by another period (byte-stuffed) to avoid confusion.
sections.eli5: Each letter gets a number. You can ask for it by number, or ask for a list of all numbers. You can say 'throw this one away' without reading it. The post office talks back with simple yes or no answers.

sections.title: Optional Commands and Variants
sections.content:
RFC 1081 defines two optional commands. The TOP command retrieves just the message headers plus a specified number of lines from the body, allowing clients to preview messages without downloading them fully. The RPOP command provides an alternate authentication method: instead of a password, a client connecting from a privileged TCP port (less than 1024) can authenticate using the sender's identity on the client host, checked via the host's .rhosts mechanism. This allowed trust-based authentication in local networks but has security drawbacks (as noted in the RFC, this feature enabled unauthorized access).

The RFC emphasizes that POP3 implementations should put intelligence in the client, not the server. Rather than having the server parse and format message data, it should send raw messages and let smart clients decide what to do with them. This keeps the server simple and allows clients to evolve independently.
sections.eli5: There are fancy ways to do extra things: ask for just the beginning of a letter, or prove you are you by your computer's identity instead of a password. But the basic idea is to keep the post office simple.

sections.title: The Split User Agent Model
sections.content:
RFC 1081 introduces the split-UA (user agent) model for email. Traditionally, a single program on a user's computer handles both sending and receiving mail. But in the split-UA model, sending and receiving are split: SMTP handles outbound mail from the workstation to a relay, and POP3 handles retrieval from the server back to the workstation. This reflects the reality that workstations are not always fully connected and cannot run a mail server.

The RFC notes that the client host appears to the mail system as a user agent only, not as a trusted mail server. This is important for security: mail sent from a workstation goes through a relay that validates it, rather than the workstation presenting mail directly as if it were the origin. The architecture enables light clients (like early PCs) to participate in Internet mail without the overhead of a full MTS implementation.
sections.eli5: One program on your computer sends mail (using SMTP), another gets mail (using POP3). This works well because your computer might not always be on, so it cannot be a full post office.
